prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem portrays Barbie Chang’s alienation, depression, romantic rejection, and vulnerability through fragmented, surreal urban imagery and relentless wordplay. Her immobilization amid indifferent men and an unprepared city reveals how loneliness, gendered violence, and self-erasure trap her in recurring cycles of mourning.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Barbie, Chang

outputs.L1:
Barbie Chang’s tears are the city lights, going off, on, off, on. The men walking around the city move, but Barbie Chang does not. She cannot promote herself. If she had legs, she would stop begging; if she had a head, she would stop her own wedding. But the city has no extra bedding. It is not ready yet; the maids are still making beds.

Barbie Chang is still making things up. There are always storms, long arms, drinks with pink umbrellas, because they know she is confused like a seahorse. Light avoids her town on the map: B2, C4. She wants to be used; she does not want to be with you.

It is morning again, and Barbie Chang is already mourning the men—the night men who are always right, who never write back. She prefers to sleep on her back so she can see the eyes of her attackers. In the morning: a bed with questions, with her depression on each side, and two small holes from knees.
outputs.L2:
The city’s lamps flicker—dark, bright, dark, bright—with Barbie Chang’s weeping. Men wander through the streets, but she remains motionless. She cannot advertise herself. Given legs, she would no longer plead; given a head, she would prevent her own marriage. Yet the city, unprepared, has no spare linens: the servants have not finished arranging the beds.

Barbie Chang continues inventing. Storms never cease. Long arms carry cocktails shaded by tiny pink parasols, aware that she is bewildered like a seahorse. Illumination passes over her town, marked B2 C4 on the map. She longs to be used, though not to stay with you.

Morning returns, and already Barbie Chang grieves for the men of darkness—the night men who are invariably correct and never answer her messages. She chooses to lie faceup, wanting to meet her assailants’ eyes when daylight comes. The bed is filled with questions; depression rests on both sides of her, beside two little hollows pressed there by knees.
outputs.L3: Barbie Chang remains emotionally immobilized even as the city—and the men around her—continues to move forward. She feels unable to advocate for herself or resist the expectations imposed upon her, and her uncertainty becomes so profound that she can no longer reliably distinguish reality from her own inventions. The city offers no meaningful refuge: it seems unprepared to shelter, support, or even acknowledge her, leaving her isolated and overlooked. At the same time, she mourns emotionally unavailable men who remain convinced of their own righteousness yet never answer her needs or respond to her pain. Her depression and fear persist even in the supposed safety of bed, where she remains watchful and tense, anticipating the possibility of attack rather than finding rest.
outputs.L4:
The poem depicts Barbie Chang as profoundly alienated from both the people around her and the urban world she inhabits. Although she moves through social spaces filled with men, crowds, buildings, and public activity, she remains emotionally isolated. The city does not offer connection or protection; instead, it appears indifferent and unprepared for her suffering. Its fragmented, surreal imagery mirrors Barbie’s depression, making the external landscape seem as unstable and disordered as her inner life.

Barbie’s romantic rejection intensifies this sense of estrangement. Her desire for intimacy is met with absence, indifference, or refusal, leaving her unable to move beyond the experience of loss. The men around her retain the freedom to act, depart, or ignore her, while Barbie becomes increasingly immobilized. This contrast exposes an unequal gendered dynamic: male detachment is treated as ordinary, but Barbie is left to bear the emotional and physical consequences of rejection. Her vulnerability therefore appears not merely personal but shaped by a world in which women’s pain is easily overlooked.

The poem’s relentless wordplay deepens this instability. Words repeat, split apart, echo one another, and acquire new meanings, preventing the language from settling into a single clear statement. Such verbal fragmentation conveys Barbie’s difficulty in understanding or expressing what has happened to her. It also suggests the compulsive nature of grief. Her mind circles the same images and feelings, trying to transform them through language but repeatedly returning to the original wound. Humor and absurdity may briefly surface in the puns, yet they do not relieve her pain; instead, they reveal how language itself can become another trap.

Barbie’s immobilization is one of the poem’s most striking expressions of depression. She seems suspended between longing and resignation, unable either to restore the lost relationship or to create a life outside it. The indifferent city offers no meaningful ritual, structure, or community through which she might process her grief. Because neither the men around her nor the larger social environment acknowledges her suffering, mourning becomes repetitive rather than restorative.

This repetition also points toward self-erasure. Barbie gradually loses a stable sense of identity as she measures herself through the attention and rejection of others. Her name evokes an artificial, culturally manufactured ideal of femininity, suggesting that she is pressured to become an object of desire even while her own desires remain unmet. The tension between being visible as a feminine image and invisible as a suffering person makes her especially vulnerable to emotional and gendered violence.

Ultimately, the poem presents loneliness as a recurring condition rather than a temporary mood. Its fractured form, surreal cityscape, and obsessive verbal patterns place the reader inside Barbie’s disorientation. Romantic rejection initiates her mourning, but social indifference sustains it. Trapped between the desire to be loved and the impulse to disappear, Barbie moves through cycles of grief in which loss is repeated, language breaks down, and the self becomes increasingly difficult to preserve.
outputs.L5:
**Barbie and Chang**

Barbie and Chang had always dreamed of creating something meaningful together. Barbie loved fashion and design, while Chang was fascinated by technology and engineering. One day, they decided to combine their talents and build a collection of stylish clothes made from recycled materials.

Barbie sketched colorful outfits, and Chang developed a small machine that could transform discarded plastic into usable fabric. Their project soon attracted attention throughout the community. Together, Barbie and Chang showed that creativity, friendship, and innovation could make the world a more beautiful and sustainable place.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about Barbie Chang wandering through a hostile city, using repetition, wordplay, dream logic, and almost no punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
barbie chang walks into the city and the city walks out of her  

the buildings bare their building teeth  
the windows wink without kindness  
every taxi says no in a yellow voice  
no no no says the rain which rises from the gutter and returns to the clouds as smoke  

barbie chang carries a purse full of doors  
she opens one and finds monday  
she opens another and finds monday wearing her face  
monday says you do not belong here  
here says the echo  
hear says the siren  
her says the street as it steals one letter at a time  

at the crosswalk the white figure refuses to walk  
the red hand grows redder  
it reaches down and searches her coat for a country  
barbie chang has only crumbs  
only names folded into smaller names  
only a mother tongue asleep beneath her tongue  

the city calls her barbie  
the city calls her chang  
the city calls her change and keeps the change  

she passes a school where the children throw shadows  
she passes a bank where the money dreams of being blood  
she passes a mirror selling better mirrors  
inside each mirror barbie chang is almost arriving  
almost alive  
almost approved  

walk says the sidewalk  
walk away says the sidewalk  
barbie chang walks until walking becomes waking  
until her shoes fill with tiny mayors  
until every mayor declares her feet illegal  

still she goes  
still she goes  
still the city shuts its thousand mouths around her  

then barbie chang opens the last door in her purse  

behind it is the same city  
smaller now  
no larger than a word  

she puts the word beneath her tongue  

the city begins to dissolve  
the city begins to listen  
the city begins again to say no  

but barbie chang has learned the grammar of no  

no is a door  
no is a road  
no is the small bright o she steps through  

and goes
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem in the style of Victoria Chang’s *Barbie Chang*, exploring loneliness, depression, rejection, and urban nightlife.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Victoria Chang’s exact style, but I can offer an original experimental poem using fragmentation, repetition, dark humor, surreal urban imagery, and social alienation.

**Nightlife Has Left the Group Chat**

At 1:13 a.m. the city says  
**seen**

but does not answer.

The woman wears a silver dress  
to resemble an emergency exit.  
Everyone passes through her.

At the bar, loneliness orders  
another loneliness. Neat.  
Depression tips twenty percent  
because depression has worked  
in service.

Outside, taxis drag their yellow  
erasers through the rain.  
Every window contains a party  
she was almost invited to.

Almost is a small nightclub.  
Almost stamps her wrist.  
Almost says not tonight.  
Almost has a beautiful mouth  
full of other people’s names.

She dances beside the speaker  
until her heart becomes  
a complaint from downstairs.

No one hears it.  
The bass has excellent boundaries.

At 2:46 a.m. she texts:  
**are you awake**

to a number that has learned  
how not to be.

The phone glows against her face,  
a tiny police interrogation:

Where were you  
when you were wanted?

She cannot remember.

The moon hangs over the rooftops  
like a pill she forgot to take.  
The buildings keep all their lights on  
but refuse to call it hope.

Morning arrives in a sanitation truck,  
lifting the night by its black plastic handles.

Inside one bag: her name.  
Inside another: the dress.  
Inside another: the little animal  
that kept asking to be chosen.

The city says  
**delivered**

The city says nothing else.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single breathless paragraph-poem about a woman named Barbie Chang who mourns men who never write back. Include beds, storms, city lights, pink umbrellas, and unsettling imagery.
counterfactuals.output: Barbie Chang keeps the beds of men who never write back neatly made inside her chest, each pillow dented by an absent head, each sheet cold as a tongue in a jar, and when storms drag their black fingernails across the windows she walks beneath the city lights with pink umbrellas blooming around her like wounded jellyfish, whispering their names into gutters where the rain has collected teeth, watching taxis smear gold across the avenue, watching her reflection follow half a second too late, and she mourns them all—the man who promised Tuesday, the man who became three dots and vanished, the man whose silence arrived nightly and sat at the foot of her bed—until every room fills with wet feathers, every lamp hums like an insect trapped in bone, and Barbie Chang lies awake while the unanswered letters climb from her phone in tiny white gowns and press their blank faces to hers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented feminist prose poem in which Barbie Chang feels immobilized and scrutinized by men, blending emotional vulnerability with absurd, associative language.
counterfactuals.output:
Barbie Chang becomes a chair when the men enter. Not sits in—becomes. Four obedient legs, one polished back, no mouth except the small wooden scream of being dragged across a floor.

They inspect her silence for pockets.

One man says posture. Another says smile. A third adjusts the weather so it falls only on women. Barbie Chang tries to lift her hand, but her hand has been declared a committee. It must deliberate. It must wait for funding.

Inside her: a rabbit made of glass. Inside the rabbit: a tiny red siren wearing lipstick.

The men discuss her as if she is an appliance left on. Too warm. Too loud. Potentially dangerous near water. Barbie Chang imagines unplugging the room.

She is vulnerable in the way a door is vulnerable: everyone believes it exists to open.

Her knees become parentheses around nothing. Her throat, an elevator refusing every floor. Still, their eyes press fingerprints onto her—forehead, waist, résumé, grief.

Barbie Chang thinks: I am not your evidence.

But the sentence crawls under the table and hides among the shoes.

So she waits, immobile as a pink planet declared decorative, while beneath her lacquered surface the oceans practice standing up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde poem with run-on syntax and recurring puns such as “morning/mourning” and “right/write,” ending with a disturbing image involving a bed, questions, and knees.
counterfactuals.output:
At morning the city puts on its mourning  
coat buttoned with windows that refuse to look out  
and I walk right through the wrong door to write  
my name on the tongue of a bell, which rings  
which wrings the hour from its damp little hands  
while the streets repeat street street as if direction  
were a stutter and every corner had forgotten  
what it was turning away from  

I say good morning, meaning forgive me  
I say good mourning, meaning don’t  
and the pigeons edit the sky with their erasers  
their wings all margin, all maybe, all  
right right right until the page bruises  
and I write left because nothing remains  
but the grammar of departure, the comma  
dragging its small black suitcase behind it  

meanwhile the sun, that unpaid actor, rises  
or lies about rising, and the roofs applaud  
with their rusted palms, and somewhere  
a clock eats its own face to save time  
somewhere a child spells home as whom  
and waits for an answer to inhabit it  

I keep walking though walking keeps me  
keeps me like a secret under the floorboards  
where every nail is a no, every plank  
a sentence sentenced to mean more  
than wood should mean, and the morning  
leans closer in its mourning veil  
to whisper you are right, so write  
you are right, so write, so wrong  

until at last the room arrives around me  
without walls, without warning, the bed  
made neatly from all the questions  
no one dared to ask, their hooks turned inward  
their question marks crawling beneath the sheet—  
and there, at the foot of it, my knees  
are already kneeling, though I am still standing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
